short: Montgomery's victory in Egypt, the first clear British land win of the war.
full:
Rommel's advance had been halted forty miles from Alexandria in July 1942 on a line anchored between the sea and the impassable Qattara Depression, so there was no flank to turn. Montgomery, given the Eighth Army in August, refused to attack until he was ready. By 23 October he had roughly 195,000 men and over a thousand tanks, many of them newly arrived American Shermans, against about 116,000 Axis troops and 550 tanks, whose fuel supply had been cut by Ultra-directed attacks on Mediterranean convoys.

A thousand guns opened at 9.40pm and engineers cleared lanes through half a million mines. Twelve days of attrition followed before Operation Supercharge broke through on 2 November. Rommel, back from sick leave, was ordered to stand fast, then withdrew regardless, retreating 1,400 miles to Tunisia. With the Torch landings in Morocco and Algeria on 8 November, North Africa was effectively decided. It was, in Churchill's phrase, not the end but perhaps the end of the beginning.
